title: Making People Glad to Do What You Want
hook: Stop selling them on what you want. Hand them the version of yes that gets them something they already wanted.
counterintuition: Most people assume persuasion means making your case better. It rarely does. The yes you actually need usually arrives the moment you stop arguing for your outcome and start describing theirs, in the words they already use about themselves.
reflectionBefore: Think back to a recent request you made that someone refused. What's the first thing you said to them?
reflectionAfter: Now reframe it. What do they personally gain by saying yes, and does that change how you'd ask next time?
keyTakeaway: Phrase orders as questions so the other person picks the action and owns it; you get the work done while they keep their pride. Save flat commands for true emergencies.

breakdown.fastRead:
Your boss steps to your desk and says, "Fix this report by five." Now picture him asking, "Could you take another look at this before five?" Same task. Different room. The first one stiffens your back. The second gets you nodding before you have decided anything.

That small switch is the whole move. A question hands the other person the steering wheel. He gets to say yes, instead of being told to. Nobody works hard for a plan handed down like a summons.

Ask when you can, and the work will come back wearing the other person's name.
breakdown.deepRead:
Henry runs a loading dock outside Cleveland. He has two ways to clear a jam. He can shout, "Move those crates now." Or he can walk over and ask, "What's the fastest way to get these out before the next truck?" The crates move either way. Only the second version leaves his crew standing a little taller, and you will see it in their backs.

The shift is small and the gain is real. A flat order tells a grown adult what to do. A question invites him to figure it out. The work gets done in both cases, but the question lets the man keep his pride. He becomes the one solving the problem, not the one being managed.

Watch what happens at home. A father can tell his teenage son, "Take out the trash." Or he can say, "The bin's getting full, what do you want to do about it?" The son who answers his own question is far more likely to stand up. He picked the action. He owns it. You did not spend Saturday afternoon arguing over a kitchen bin.

There is a trade-off, and say it out loud. In an emergency, you give the order. A burning kitchen is not the moment to poll the line cook on the fire extinguisher. Seconds count, dignity waits.

Most days you have the seconds. Use them.
breakdown.fullRead:
A young manager named Ruth learns this her first month on the job. She tells a forty-year veteran of the warehouse exactly how to stack a pallet, the way the manual says, and she does it in front of three of his coworkers. He stacks it her way. He also stops volunteering for anything for the next six weeks. She won the pallet and lost the man.

What went wrong was not the content of her instruction. The pallet probably did need fixing. The form did the damage. She gave a grown adult an order in front of his peers, which is the one thing almost nobody forgets. The fix would have cost her a single sentence: "You've stacked more of these than I ever will, what do you think we should do here?" Same outcome. Different man at the end of it. Six weeks of willingness she could have kept.

So here is the move. Turn the order into a question, and let the other person walk himself to the answer. You lose nothing. The work still gets done. You gain the one thing you can never order into existence, which is willingness.

A question does three quiet things at once. It treats the other person as someone with a brain worth consulting. It hands him authorship of whatever happens next, so he defends the plan instead of resenting it. And it leaves you a way out if his answer is better than yours, which it sometimes will be. An order does none of that. An order is a closed door, and the person on the other side of it remembers the sound.

Consider a dentist with a nervous patient in the chair. She can say, "Open wider." She can also say, "Can you give me a little more room here?" The jaw opens the same number of millimeters. But the patient who was asked feels like a partner in the procedure, not a specimen on a tray. She books her cleaning next year. The one who was commanded books with someone else.

Now the honest caveat. Questions are not always the right tool. A pilot does not poll the cabin on whether to lower the landing gear. A surgeon does not ask the resident how she feels about the next incision. When the stakes are high and the time is short and the roles are clear, a direct instruction is the kind thing, because it lifts the burden of choice off people who do not need it. The skill is knowing which room you are standing in.

Most of the time, you are not in the cockpit or the operating room. You are at a kitchen table, a project meeting, a Saturday morning with a teenager who will not get out of bed. In those rooms, the question almost always beats the order. Not because it is softer, but because it is more honest about who is doing the work. The other person is. You are only shaping the ask.

Hand him the pen, and let him sign his own name to the plan.

examples.title: Pernilla Asks Margery to Trade Rooms Without Asking

planSpec.domain: a school principal asking a beloved fourth-grade teacher to give up her classroom and move to a smaller room down the hall
planSpec.audience: a public-school principal handling a midyear room reshuffle
planSpec.stakes: keeping the teacher's morale intact while making space for a new specialist program parents have been demanding
planSpec.requiredBeat: the principal opens by naming, in the teacher's own language, why the new room actually suits the teacher's pride in her work, and the teacher volunteers for the move before being asked

examples.scenario: Pernilla finds Margery stacking spelling tests in room 14 after dismissal. 'You've told me twice this year the back wall eats half the kids' writing in glare, and that you wish you had more pinning room.' Margery laughs. 'Every afternoon by two.' 'Room 8 down the hall has a long north wall. No glare. Smaller, but every inch is wall.' Margery sets down the stack. 'Is fourteen going to the specialist program?' Pernilla nods. 'Then let me move into 8.'
examples.whatToDo: Open with the complaint she has already voiced about her own room, the glare, the lost pinning space, and describe room 8 as the fix. Then wait. Let her name the move.
examples.whyItMatters: A request that solves a problem the listener has already named out loud lands as relief, not loss. Authorship transfers the moment her own grievance becomes the reason to move.

examples.title: Lourdes Stops Reciting Fall Statistics to Stanley

planSpec.domain: a hospice nurse persuading a stubborn 82-year-old patient to start using a walker he refuses to touch
planSpec.audience: a hospice nurse on a home visit
planSpec.stakes: the patient's next fall will likely break a hip and end his ability to live at home, which is the one thing he says he wants
planSpec.requiredBeat: the nurse stops listing safety reasons and instead frames the walker as the tool that lets him keep walking his dog to the mailbox alone, and he reaches for it himself

examples.scenario: Lourdes is on her third home visit with Stanley, 82, whose aluminum walker leans against the kitchen wall like a thing he refuses to be introduced to. She has tried fall statistics, hip-fracture rates, the ER bill. He stares at the linoleum. She stops mid-sentence. Her eyes find the leash on the back-door hook. 'You said the best part of your morning is walking the dog to the mailbox alone.' Stanley's chin lifts. 'This walker keeps that walk yours.' His hand moves toward the grip before she finishes.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the safety lecture. Name the one specific freedom he has told you he wants, and frame the walker as the only thing that protects it. Then go quiet and let him reach.
examples.whyItMatters: Pride defends itself harder than reason persuades. Once the request becomes the protection of his own stated wish, refusing it would mean refusing himself, and that is a fight he will not pick.

examples.title: Garth Calls Levi the Night Before Black Friday

planSpec.domain: a small-town hardware store owner asking his weekend stock clerk to come in early on Black Friday
planSpec.audience: the owner of a family hardware store
planSpec.stakes: a no costs him the busiest morning of the year; a heavy-handed ask costs him a clerk who has other job offers
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner names a specific thing the clerk has said he wants — Saturday afternoons free to coach his sister's soccer team — and shapes the early shift as the trade that protects it

examples.scenario: It is 9:14 p.m. Wednesday, and Garth sits at the back counter of his hardware store with the Black Friday schedule under one hand and his phone under the other. He needs Levi, his weekend stock clerk, on the floor at 4 a.m. Levi has two other job offers and has said three times this fall that the one thing he will not give up is afternoons free to coach his kid sister's soccer team. Garth's thumb hovers over the call button. He has to decide, right now, whether to ask in his own terms or in Levi's.
examples.whatToDo: Frame the dawn-to-noon shift as the trade that ends before practice and protects the coaching afternoons through the whole holiday stretch, then ask Levi if that swap is the cleanest way to keep them clear.
examples.whyItMatters: People agree fast when the request is already shaped around what they were going to defend anyway. Levi's no would have been about the soccer team. The yes is the same answer to the same worry.

examples.title: Mathias trades the custody speech for Annika's audition list

planSpec.domain: a divorced father asking his thirteen-year-old daughter to spend Sunday afternoons doing homework at his apartment instead of her mother's
planSpec.audience: a divorced father navigating shared custody
planSpec.stakes: if he pushes, she resents him; if he gives up, her grades keep slipping and her mother blames him for it
planSpec.requiredBeat: the father stops citing the custody schedule and instead points to the daughter's stated wish to make the high-school orchestra audition, framing his quieter apartment as the place that gets her there

examples.scenario: Mathias sits across the kitchen table from his thirteen-year-old, Annika, on a Sunday afternoon. Her viola case is open, the Sibelius score weighted with a salt shaker. He had rehearsed a small speech about the custody calendar and what her mother's lawyer said it allowed. He sets it aside. The high-school orchestra audition list goes up in three weeks. Her younger brother and the dog are at her mother's. Here there is only the metronome and the kitchen clock. He tells her, plainly, that this is the room that gets her in.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the schedule argument. Frame Sunday afternoons at his apartment as the quiet hours that get her ready for the audition she has been talking about, then ask once in those terms.
examples.whyItMatters: A thirteen-year-old will fight a rule and protect a goal. Tying the ask to her own ambition turns compliance into something she chooses for herself, which is the only kind that lasts past next Sunday.

examples.title: Rutger Reflects on the Route Nobody Wanted

planSpec.domain: a city bus dispatcher asking a senior driver to take on a new route nobody wants, through a neighborhood with chronic schedule problems
planSpec.audience: a transit dispatcher with thirty years on the job
planSpec.stakes: if the senior driver refuses, the route falls to a rookie who will likely quit within a month, and the dispatcher loses a route and a driver
planSpec.requiredBeat: the dispatcher reflects on a previous time he ordered the assignment and lost the driver, then describes the conversation where he instead named the senior driver's reputation for fixing broken routes and got a yes within two minutes

examples.scenario: Rutger has been dispatching at the Linwood depot for thirty-one years. Last spring he ordered Halton onto the troubled crosstown route and lost him to the suburban transit company within a month. Now Route 41 is open again, the same chronic mess, and Sims is sitting across the desk with his thermos. Rutger does not order. He says, "Sims, when a route is broken, the only driver I trust to read it inside a week is you. Nobody else on this board has put a sick line back on schedule the way you did with the 19." Sims sets the thermos down. Two minutes later he is asking which shift he starts.
examples.whatToDo: Name the specific reputation the person has earned, then frame the unwanted task as the one thing only that reputation can fix, and let them claim it.
examples.whyItMatters: A senior worker's hardest-won asset is standing among peers. Tie the ask to that standing and the yes is no longer a favor to you, it is a deposit into something they already protect.

examples.title: Etta Asks Jovita What the Duck Should Do

planSpec.domain: a wedding caterer asking a head chef to switch from her preferred plated entrée to a family-style service the bride suddenly wants three weeks out
planSpec.audience: a wedding caterer running a four-person kitchen
planSpec.stakes: the chef has artistic pride in the plated dish and may walk; the wedding pays a quarter of the year's revenue
planSpec.requiredBeat: the caterer asks the chef what she would most want a guest to remember about the meal, and shapes the family-style switch as the format that delivers exactly that, so the chef proposes the change herself

examples.scenario: Etta corners Jovita at the prep table three weeks before the Hollander wedding. The bride has phoned twice asking for family-style. Jovita is fanning duck slices on a tasting plate like a card trick. 'Before I say anything else, what do you most want a guest to walk out remembering?' 'That they've never tasted a duck like that one.' 'Now picture two long tables. The bird on a board down the middle, people reaching in.' Jovita's tweezers stop. 'We could carve it whole, at the table,' she says.
examples.whatToDo: Ask Jovita what she most wants a guest to remember, listen for the answer in her own words, and then describe family-style as the form that delivers exactly that. Let her propose the switch.
examples.whyItMatters: A chef defends the format she chose, not the outcome she actually wanted. Move the talk to the outcome in her own words, and the format becomes hers to revise. The yes you need is the one she arrives at.

questions.prompt: A restaurant manager wants the night dishwasher to take on a few hours of prep work before service. The dishwasher has talked openly about wanting to learn to cook so he can one day run his own food truck. What opening lands best?
choices: If you do prep with me before service, you pick up the knife skills and timing you will need to actually run that food truck.
Starting next week you will help with prep before service so the line moves faster on busy nights.
I need a hand with prep and since you are already here, you might as well take it on.
questions.explanation: He has named a goal of his own, the food truck. Tying prep work to skills he already wants makes saying yes feel like progress. The schedule order ignores his motivation, and 'might as well' offers him nothing he is reaching for.

questions.prompt: A small-town librarian wants a recently retired neighbor to lead Saturday storytime for young children. The retiree has said in passing that she misses being around her grandchildren, who moved out of state last year. Which opening is strongest?
choices: We really need a volunteer and you are the most reliable person on the schedule.
Storytime puts you in a room of small kids every Saturday morning, which sounds like the piece of life with the grandkids you said you missed.
It is only thirty minutes a week and most of the books you would already know.
questions.explanation: She has told you what she lost, time among small children. Pointing storytime at exactly that gap makes the yes serve her, not the library. Reliability and brevity are reasons that matter to the building, not to her.

questions.prompt: A youth soccer coach is asking a fifteen-year-old to attend optional Saturday practices. The player has said her single goal is making the varsity team next fall. Which approach is most likely to backfire?
choices: Tell her honestly that these Saturdays are the gap between players who make varsity and players who do not.
Ask her which skills she thinks varsity coaches will be watching for, then describe Saturday practice as the place to sharpen those.
Tell her the team needs the numbers and you are counting on her sense of commitment to show up.
questions.explanation: Headcount and commitment are reasons that serve the coach, not her. The other two openings tie Saturdays to the varsity goal she has already named. Reasons that serve only the asker tend to feel like pressure rather than offer.

questions.prompt: A veterinary practice manager wants a senior tech to train a difficult new hire. The senior tech has said for months she wants to be promoted to lead tech the next time the position opens. How should the manager open?
choices: Training the new hire is what gets you in front of the doctors as the person they trust to bring people up, and that is how lead techs get picked here.
Can you train the new hire? Nobody else has your patience and you are the senior person on the floor.
I am assigning the training to you because you have the longest tenure and that is how it works.
questions.explanation: She wants to be promoted. Framing the training as the visible work the doctors notice connects the ask to her stated goal. Patience and tenure are the manager's reasons, not hers, so they read as a burden to absorb rather than a step she gains from.

questions.prompt: You want a colleague to take on a project nobody else has volunteered for. Which option best captures the move of asking in terms of what the colleague gains?
choices: List every reason the project matters to the company, the customer, and the team in priority order.
Find something the colleague already wants for themselves and show how saying yes moves them closer to it, then ask in those words.
Apologize for the imposition and offer extra time off so the project feels like less of a sacrifice.
questions.explanation: The move is to connect the ask to a goal the other person already holds. Reasons in your priority order are your case, not theirs. Apology with compensation treats the work as pure cost rather than a path toward anything they actually want.

questions.prompt: A factory floor supervisor wants his most experienced welder to mentor a struggling new hire. For months that welder has been openly saying he is tired of training people and wants to focus only on his own work. Why might 'you are the best teacher we have' backfire?
choices: Because the welder will accept any compliment and agree to almost anything that follows it.
Because praise without money attached almost never produces a real yes.
Because the welder has said he wants the opposite of more teaching, and the ask must connect to what he wants now, not to a flattering picture of his past.
questions.explanation: He has stated his current goal, less training, not more. Praising him as a great teacher reaches for the version of him he is trying to leave behind. The first two distractors misread the moment as a question about flattery or pay rather than alignment with his actual goal.

questions.prompt: A charity board member is asking a local restaurateur to donate two hundred meals for a fundraising dinner. The restaurateur has been telling everyone who will listen that nobody knows his restaurant moved to a new street last spring. What opening is strongest?
choices: Your name will be on the program, called from the stage, and printed on every flyer, which puts your new address in front of three hundred local families in one evening.
Two hundred meals is a lot, but it is for a worthy cause and we are running out of places to ask.
Two of your competitors donated last year, so it would look odd in town if you did not.
questions.explanation: He has named the problem he wants solved, that nobody knows his new location. Showing him the visibility the donation buys ties the ask to that exact problem. Worthy causes and competitor comparisons offer nothing he is presently trying to fix.

questions.prompt: A high school chemistry teacher wants a busy parent to help with monthly lab cleanups. The parent has said her hours at work are long, and she has also said she wishes she had more sense of her son's school day. Which framing serves her best?
choices: Honestly, nobody else has stepped up and we are getting desperate enough to call parents one by one.
Cleanup runs the period right before pickup, so you would already be in the building, see your son's lab, and catch his classmates filing out.
Could you take it as a favor to me, since we have always gotten along well at conferences?
questions.explanation: She has said she wants a window into her son's day. Pinning cleanup to the hour right before pickup gives her exactly that window. Desperation and personal favors connect to your needs and the relationship, not to anything she has told you she wants.

questions.prompt: An office manager needs a senior accountant to learn the new bookkeeping software the firm just adopted. He has dismissed the change and resents younger staff treating him as out of date. Which opening is strongest?
choices: If you learn the new system early, the partners will look on you favorably at review time.
The partners want everyone trained by quarter end, so you cannot keep working on the old system.
You said last week you were tired of younger staff bringing you software questions; if you learn this first, those questions come through you and you set the pace.
questions.explanation: He resents being treated as behind. Framing early mastery as the way he stays the room's senior expert reaches the position he actually wants. Review threats and quarter-end mandates land as pressure and confirm the very status worry he is already feeling.

reviewCards.front: You need a coworker to take on a task they will dislike. Before you ask, what is the one thing you must figure out?
reviewCards.back: Find what the coworker personally gains by saying yes, then phrase the request in those terms. The move is to reframe the ask around their wants, not yours, so the answer feels like a choice that serves them.

reviewCards.front: Your teenager refuses to clean her room. You have already explained why it matters to you. What should you try instead?
reviewCards.back: Stop citing your reasons and name something she has told you she wants, like having friends over without embarrassment, then shape the cleanup as the path to that. Ask in her terms, not yours, and let her see the gain before you make the request.

reviewCards.front: A neighbor asks you to water her plants for two weeks while she travels. She lists how much it would help her. Why is this ask weak, and how would you fix it?
reviewCards.back: She is selling her gain, not yours. The fix is to find what you would personally value, a spare key for emergencies, her tomatoes while she is gone, a favor banked for later, and to frame the request in those terms so saying yes serves you too.

reviewCards.front: You are a volunteer coordinator. A reliable parent has stopped showing up. You need her back for the spring fundraiser. What do you say first?
reviewCards.back: Open by naming, in her own words, what she has told you she gets out of the work, maybe seeing her son lead the booth or being the person other parents turn to, then shape the fundraiser as the next chance to do that. The yes follows when she sees her own gain restated.

reviewCards.front: A family member is wrong about a medical decision and you need them to reverse course. Listing the medical risks has not worked. What is the move?
reviewCards.back: Stop pressing the risks and find the outcome they personally want, staying in their own home, walking their grandchild down the aisle, keeping their independence, then frame the reversal as the thing that protects that outcome. Ask in those terms and let them choose the result they already want.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You are learning to translate your ask into the other person's currency before you open your mouth. The skill is finding the specific thing they already want, naming it in their own words, and shaping your request as the path to it. With practice, this becomes automatic, you stop pitching what you need and start pointing at what they get.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to assign a task no one wants, then before you ask, write down one thing the person has said matters to them this quarter and lead with how the task protects or advances it.
If you catch yourself about to say because I said so or because we agreed, then stop, name the thing the other person actually wants from this week, and reshape your request as the route to that.

If you are pushing a family member to use a cane, take a pill, or see a doctor and they keep refusing, then drop the safety argument and tie the action to the one independence they have told you they fear losing.
If a friend or neighbor is dragging their feet on a favor, then before you remind them again, ask yourself what they would brag about doing, and rephrase the favor in those terms.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one request you have been postponing because you know it will land badly. Before you send it, write two sentences naming what the other person personally gains by saying yes, then rewrite the ask so those two sentences come first.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, pick the hardest ask on your plate and run it through a one-page rewrite. Top half, what you want and why. Bottom half, what the other person wants and how your request gets them closer to it. Send only the bottom half.

memorableLines.text: An order is a closed door, and the person on the other side of it remembers the sound.
memorableLines.why: A vivid image that names what lingers after a command—not the order itself, but the memory of the tone.

memorableLines.text: You gain the one thing you can never order into existence, which is willingness.
memorableLines.why: The chapter's core paradox compressed: you can force behavior but never ownership, a truth that lands through structure.

memorableLines.text: Hand him the pen, and let him sign his own name to the plan.
memorableLines.why: Transforms compliance into ownership through a tangible gesture readers can visualize—the moment management becomes trust.
